track: Track E adjacent authoritative clinical and safeguarding guidance
journal_volume_issue_year: NICE guideline NG10, 2015; current published guidance checked 2026-08-15; full update in development
article_title: Violence and aggression: short-term management in mental health, health and community settings
author: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence
community_group: NHS mental health, health, community, emergency, and child and adolescent mental health settings
source_access: official recommendations, 2024 surveillance decision, and 2026 update-project record inspected
evidence_type: current authoritative practice guidance with a separately identified ongoing full update
exact_factual_observation: For children and young people, NG10 calls for developmentally specific trained staff, safeguarding, involvement of the child and people with parental responsibility, assessment of underlying mental-health needs, conduct history, triggers, trauma, communication, language, cognitive, and cultural factors, and de-escalation before restriction. Restrictive interventions are last resort, require continuous wellbeing monitoring, and cannot use parent contact, social interaction, food, fluids, or corporal punishment to force compliance. Seclusion decisions require senior-doctor approval and early multidisciplinary review. After restrictive intervention, the guidance separates immediate debrief from a service-user-led external review with staff from outside the ward, as soon as possible and within 72 hours, followed by a report and governing-body oversight.
what_source_establishes: A professional child-safety system distinguishes observation, assessment, immediate protection, least-restrictive intervention, debrief, independent review, plan correction, and governance reporting. It explicitly preserves development, safeguarding, family involvement, dignity, and nonpunitive rights rather than collapsing them into a danger label.
what_source_does_not_establish: The guideline is normative practice guidance, not a comparative outcome evaluation. It does not establish that every recommended component reduces violence, define legal authority outside its jurisdictions, authorize a private community to restrain, seclude, medicate, investigate, or adjudicate, or turn a clinical risk assessment into an admissions or membership screen. NICE has selected NG10 for full update, with replacement expected in 2027; provisional update material is not final guidance.
author_interpretation: NICE frames safety and dignity as joint priorities, restrictive measures as exceptional and rights-limited, and post-incident learning as both immediate and externally reviewed rather than solely internal.
alternative_interpretation: Effectiveness depends on law, staffing, training, clinical capacity, reporting integrity, advocacy, and an actually independent review body. A formal checklist without these institutions could reproduce internal control under procedural language.
response_process: Observe and document conduct and context; use trained developmental and clinical assessment; safeguard and de-escalate; use restriction only within lawful professional authority and after alternatives fail; monitor continuously; debrief after harm is contained; obtain external service-user-led review within 72 hours; amend plans and report outcomes to governance.
outcome: The guideline specifies process and monitoring outcomes but supplies no unit-level causal estimate. Its update status requires re-verification before practical reliance after the replacement is published.
transferability: High for identifying functions that must remain separate and for the floor of child rights, review, and measurement. Low for direct transfer of professional or statutory powers to intentional communities. Residents may document observable conduct, protect immediate safety within ordinary law, preserve evidence, and contact qualified or emergency services; they may not self-license clinical or coercive authority.
likely_article_destination: Non-waivable child rights / community as therapist / fair process / outcome dashboard / dangerous-child branch
notes: Current guidance status is time-sensitive. Re-check NICE's final replacement after its expected 28 January 2027 publication. Do not operationalize medication, restraint, seclusion, diagnosis, or statutory safeguarding from this ledger row.

track: Track E adjacent forensic and clinical structured-professional-judgment validation
article_title: The predictive validity of the Structured Assessment of Violence Risk in Youth (SAVRY) among institutionalised adolescents
author: Monica Gammelgård; Anna-Maija Koivisto; Markku Eronen; Riittakerttu Kaltiala-Heino
community_group: 208 adolescents in general residential adolescent psychiatry, correctional schools, or adolescent forensic units
page_locator: article pp. 352-370; publisher abstract and results summary
source_access: publisher primary record, abstract, DOI, and Tampere University publication record inspected
evidence_type: record-based short-term predictive validation with a forward six-month institutional-outcome window
exact_factual_observation: The study derived SAVRY information from medical files and child-welfare records for 208 institutionalized adolescents and examined recorded institutional violence during the following six months or until earlier discharge. After adjustment for sex, age, diagnosis, service level, and follow-up time, the reported odds ratios for institutional violence were 27.85 for the high summary-risk group and 3.83 for the moderate group relative to the low group.
what_source_establishes: A developmentally specific structured-professional-judgment process using multiple records can distinguish groups with materially different rates of recorded short-term institutional violence, even after several measured covariates are considered.
what_source_does_not_establish: The reported odds ratios are not individual probabilities and do not provide the complete confusion matrix, calibration, consequences of false positives and false negatives, subgroup performance, intervention assignment, victim outcomes, or proof that using SAVRY improves safety. File-derived ratings and institutional incident records do not establish performance in community life or intentional communities.
author_interpretation: The authors interpret SAVRY as a useful professional aid across several service levels while calling for more evidence about gender and psychopathology effects.
alternative_interpretation: Shared documentation practices, institutional surveillance, case mix, prior management, unmeasured severity, or record completeness may contribute to the association. A large relative odds ratio can coexist with low positive predictive value when events are uncommon and cannot justify a categorical label for a particular child.
response_process: Baseline record review; professional structured judgment; low, moderate, or high summary rating; forward six-month incident-record window; covariate-adjusted comparison.
outcome: Higher summary-risk groups had higher adjusted odds of recorded institutional violence. The source does not test whether assessment changed treatment, restriction, recurrence, or later community outcomes.
transferability: Medium for routing serious concerns to trained, developmentally informed independent assessment and insisting on outcome-specific validation. Low for direct intentional-community transfer and zero for a lay-created screen, automated cutoff, diagnosis, punishment, or membership decision.
likely_article_destination: Child safeguarding / outcome dashboard / dangerous-child branch / limits of screening
notes: The promoted facts are bounded to the publisher's primary abstract and verified bibliographic record. Inspect the complete article and the licensed manual before any professional application; do not reproduce proprietary instrument items or treat relative odds as individual certainty.

track: Track E adjacent secure-youth-care structured-professional-judgment field validation
article_title: Prospective Field Validation of the START:AV in a Dutch Secure Youth Care Sample
author: Tamara L. F. De Beuf; Vivienne de Vogel; Nick J. Broers; Corine de Ruiter
community_group: 106 adolescents in one 98-bed Dutch medium- and high-secure civil youth-care service
page_locator: article pp. 633-650; methods, Tables 3-8, limitations, conflict disclosure, and appendix
source_access: open primary article, tables, appendix, supplement links, DOI, and conflict disclosure inspected
evidence_type: preregistered prospective field validation with trained clinicians and blinded incident coding over four months
exact_factual_observation: Thirteen trained treatment coordinators completed final-version Dutch START:AV assessments as part of practice. A blinded research assistant coded 3,065 incidents from 21,572 progress notes and 106 treatment reports during the next four months. Final risk judgments significantly discriminated physical aggression, institutional violation, substance use, self-injury, and victimization, but not nonviolent offenses, unauthorized leave, or health neglect. Total scores had limited predictive validity; their interrater reliability was poor in a 30-case check. For tested outcomes, final judgments added no significant predictive value over lifetime history.
what_source_establishes: Structured professional judgment is outcome-specific, time-limited, dependent on trained evaluators and information quality, and requires reassessment. Field performance can be materially weaker and less reliable than a label such as validated suggests; historical behavior may dominate supposedly dynamic judgment.
what_source_does_not_establish: The study does not show that START:AV use reduced incidents, improved child wellbeing, improved victim safety, or reduced liberty-restricting measures. It is one secure civil-care service with a modest sample, high event base rates, excluded early discharges, limited subgroup power, and a mismatch between community-framed final judgments and inpatient outcomes. It does not validate lay assessment or transfer to intentional communities.
author_interpretation: The authors describe partial short-term field validity and potential use in treatment and furlough or discharge decisions while explicitly calling for research on whether the instrument improves risk-management outcomes.
alternative_interpretation: Predictive associations may reflect lifetime history, the secure setting, documentation intensity, evaluator practice, or case selection. Some high AUCs concern locally defined institutional violations; statistical discrimination does not prove clinical utility, fair decisions, or causal prevention.
response_process: Qualified multi-source assessment; outcome-specific final judgments; four-month reassessment horizon; blinded prospective incident coding; interrater, predictive, and incremental-validity checks; decision use within a licensed secure-care service.
outcome: Some final judgments discriminated later inpatient outcomes, while others did not; total scores were limited, agreement problems were material, and no tested final judgment added significant value over lifetime history for the outcomes with enough events.
transferability: High for requiring professional training, multiple information sources, short review intervals, outcome-specific uncertainty, reliability audits, and management-effect evaluation. Low for direct intentional-community transfer and zero for self-administered personality, membership, productivity, or dangerousness screening.
likely_article_destination: Child safeguarding / outcome dashboard / dangerous-child branch / limits of screening
notes: The first author worked for the institution that publishes and trains on the Dutch guide; three authors translated it, though they reported no royalties and no study funding. The instrument's content is not reproduced.

track: Track E adjacent child and adolescent inpatient post-incident review implementation
article_title: Impact of a debrief tool in acute child and adolescent mental health inpatient units: a centre's experience
author: William Billal Shepherd; Kyna Patterson; Jessica Blake; Danielle Ward; Ashlee Clarke; Cristina Diaz-Navarro; Farah Abdulsatar
community_group: acute child and adolescent mental-health inpatient units at one Canadian centre
page_locator: open article; purpose, methodology, findings, limitations, and conclusions
source_access: open primary quality-improvement article and DOI record inspected
evidence_type: single-centre quality-improvement implementation with monthly behavioral-event rate and severity plus informal staff feedback
exact_factual_observation: The centre implemented staff-requested TALK debriefs after patient behavioral events in July 2022. TALK structures a target, analysis of what went well and could improve, learning points, actions, and delegated follow-up. Monthly event rate and the share causing or nearly causing harm did not significantly decline after implementation. Informal staff feedback described emotional and learning benefits, team conversation, identification of least-restrictive and privacy issues, and patient concerns being reflected in updated care plans. Patients were not involved in the project or debriefs, tool use was inconsistent, and fewer debriefs occurred during workload surges.
what_source_establishes: Post-event review can surface staff impact, patient-care concerns, action ownership, and plan changes even when it does not reduce event frequency or severity. Review-process outcomes and safety-event outcomes must be measured separately.
what_source_does_not_establish: The uncontrolled project does not establish that TALK caused the qualitative benefits, that care-plan changes were completed or effective, or that debriefing prevents violence. Feedback was informal and unquantified; burnout and patient satisfaction were not measured; patients were not direct participants; debrief frequency and fidelity were not consistently reported; and a staff self-debrief is not independent external review.
author_interpretation: The authors conclude that standardized debriefing shows promise for learning and staff wellbeing but did not improve event rate or severity and should be studied with patient involvement and quantified outcomes.
alternative_interpretation: Positive feedback may reflect selection among staff who used the tool, QI champion influence, concurrent changes, or social desirability. Lack of event reduction may reflect inconsistent use, staff-only design, workload, insufficient follow-up, or a review mechanism that does not alter upstream conditions.
response_process: Patient behavioral event; optional staff-requested TALK debrief; analyze care; identify learning; assign actions; update care plans where concerns arise; track monthly event rate and severity; collect informal staff feedback.
outcome: No significant reduction in behavioral-event rate or severity; qualitative reports of staff support, learning, team conversation, and some care-plan updates; no direct child-reported or independently verified outcome.
transferability: High for separating immediate support, learning review, independent investigation, child participation, action completion, and safety outcomes. Medium for a simple review scaffold. Low for claiming prevention and zero for treating internal debrief as independent adjudication.
likely_article_destination: Fair process / community as therapist / outcome dashboard / child safeguarding
notes: This negative safety result is promoted because it prevents overclaim. A community review process should not be credited with prevention merely because participants find it supportive or because plans are discussed.
